question: What remains recognisable when a funeral march changes its pace and weight?
intro: A solo trumpet establishes the funeral march that opens Mahler’s Fifth. Its measured tread gives way to two contrasting episodes before the procession dwindles into isolated calls.

sections.label: Fanfare and funeral march
sections.mNote: trumpet signal frames the measured string melody

sections.label: First episode · sudden vehemence
sections.mNote: faster motion and trumpet melody interrupt the procession

sections.label: Fanfare and march restored
sections.mNote: opening rhythm returns before the heavier march resumes

sections.label: Second episode · lament
sections.mNote: episode material returns more slowly and gathers weight

sections.label: Coda · procession recedes
sections.mNote: fanfare fragments remain as the orchestral body withdraws

cues.title: A trumpet before the march
cues.text: Mahler begins with an unaccompanied trumpet, not the whole orchestra. Its repeated-note triplets and dotted rhythms supply a signal that will interrupt and reconnect the movement’s larger spans.
cues.evidence: Peters score, plate 9015, p. 3: solo first trumpet. The analysis shows a very quiet opening followed by rising level through 0:05–0:25; no precise orchestral entry is claimed.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: The signal acquires weight
cues.text: The opening grows from a single line into a much heavier statement. Keep the short repeated notes in mind: their rhythm remains recognisable when the orchestral sound expands around them.
cues.evidence: The report marks a boundary at 0:22 and high relative levels through 0:25–0:50; 0:35 is among its loudest windows. The trumpet rhythm comes from the score, not instrument separation.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: Two string registers meet
cues.text: In the march melody, Mahler brings low violins and high cellos close together. Listen for a connected singing line above the separate steps of the accompaniment, rather than treating every dotted figure as another trumpet call.
cues.evidence: Lew Smoley’s movement guide describes the first-violin and cello pairing. The report’s quiet 1:10–2:00 span supports this broad placement, not an entry time: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/listening-guide/listening-guide-movement-1-trauermarsch-funeral-march-in-gemessenem-schritt-streng-wie-ein-kondukt/
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Summer work at Maiernigg
cues.text: Mahler writes the Fifth during the summers of 1901 and 1902, chiefly at Maiernigg on the Wörthersee. His conducting work in Vienna makes the summer months his principal time for composition.
cues.evidence: Composition dates and Maiernigg: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-5/symphony-no-5-introduction/. The composer biography records his Vienna Court Opera post and summer working routine.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: A renewed orchestral swell
cues.text: The measured music has room for another forceful rise without abandoning its processional character. Follow the ascent and the quieter space after it as one large phrase.
cues.evidence: Relative level rises from −29.5 dB at 2:05 to −9.6 at 2:30, then falls to −25.7 by 2:55; novelty also peaks at 2:40. This describes the recorded contour only.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: A march can sing
cues.text: Across the quieter stretches, distinguish the sustained melody from the short accompaniment. A funeral march need not consist entirely of detached notes: Mahler places a legato phrase inside its regular tread.
cues.evidence: The score and Smoley’s guide distinguish the string march melody from its dotted-rhythm accompaniment. The report places a comparatively even, quiet span at 3:00–3:55; no individual note is located.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Colour without a new pulse
cues.text: The opening span passes melodic responsibility between strings and woodwinds. Listen for a change in colour that does not necessarily mean a new tempo or a new theme.
cues.evidence: Peters p. 14 shows flute, oboe and clarinet lines with cellos, above the march accompaniment. The 4:02 boundary and comparatively subdued 4:00–4:25 windows provide an approximate passage anchor, not a bar alignment.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Illness is not a programme
cues.text: Mahler suffers a serious haemorrhage in February 1901, before the Fifth’s first composing summer. That chronology does not make this march a documented account of the illness: the score gives a musical genre, not a named event.
cues.evidence: The illness and composition chronology are recorded at https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-5/symphony-no-5-introduction/. No causal autobiographical programme is asserted.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: The first interruption
cues.text: The first contrasting episode replaces the measured procession with much more urgent motion. The trumpet has a longer line to project against the moving strings; the contrast is in pace and texture as well as volume.
cues.evidence: The strongest boundary is at 5:18, with level rising from −26.3 dB at 5:15 to −12.0 at 5:20. Peters pp. 20–25 and Smoley’s guide identify the first, B♭-minor episode and its trumpet/string opposition.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Melody against moving figures
cues.text: Through the faster episode, separate the longer melodic shapes from the shorter notes underneath. The moving accompaniment can make the surface feel crowded even while the main phrase stretches across several beats.
cues.evidence: Peters p. 25 shows the prominent trumpet line over moving violin figures. The report remains at relatively high levels throughout 5:20–6:45; the note describes the episode generally.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Pressure before the return
cues.text: This episode pushes towards a strong crest and then loses weight. Listen across the retreat: a return can be prepared by withdrawing sound, not only by adding a louder announcement.
cues.evidence: The report lists 6:35 and 6:45 among the loudest windows, followed by a fall to −23.0 dB at 7:00 and boundaries at 6:52 and 6:58.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: Recognition through rhythm
cues.text: The returning fanfare restores the opening’s rhythmic identity before the funeral march settles back into place. Compare the repeated-note call with its first appearance, now heard after the faster episode.
cues.evidence: The 6:58 change and the renewed swell at 7:15–7:25 support an approximate fanfare-return region. Smoley describes the fanfare as the bridge into the returning A section; this is not a precise thematic alignment.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Heavy need not mean loud
cues.text: Mahler marks the returning march “Schwer” — heavy. The instruction concerns the weight of the phrase as well as its loudness; listen for deliberate movement through a quieter orchestral texture.
cues.evidence: Peters p. 33, rehearsal 12, marks Schwer with quiet woodwinds, brass and lower strings. The report drops sharply at 7:40–7:50 and remains subdued around 8:00–8:15; placement is provisional.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Cologne hears the Fifth
cues.text: Mahler conducts the symphony’s premiere in Cologne on 18 October 1904. The five movements are grouped into three parts: this march and the stormy second movement together form Part I.
cues.evidence: Premiere: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-5/symphony-no-5-history/. Three-part grouping: the Peters score and https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-5/symphony-no-5-introduction/.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: The return thins out
cues.text: The returning span retreats towards one of the movement’s quietest stretches. Keep following the phrase through that loss of weight rather than hearing the low level as a break in the argument.
cues.evidence: Strong boundaries at 9:20 and 9:34 accompany a broad decline from −22.1 dB at 9:15 to −46.6 at 9:50. No literal silence is asserted.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: An episode reconsidered
cues.text: The second episode recalls the earlier contrasting material without simply restoring its speed. Its more song-like treatment brings the episode closer to the funeral march that surrounds it.
cues.evidence: Smoley describes the second trio as a slower transformation of the first trio’s trumpet theme. The 9:50 trough and rise through 10:00–10:20 support the approximate 9:56 section anchor; machine key labels are not used to identify the melody.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Long notes gather force
cues.text: In this later span, follow the sustained melodic line across the changing weight beneath it. The approach to a climax can stretch a phrase as well as intensify its accompaniment.
cues.evidence: The second-trio account in Smoley’s guide describes increasingly sustained, weighty writing. The report rises through 10:35–11:10; the listening instruction makes no claim about a particular instrument at 10:40.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The largest recorded crest
cues.text: The later episode reaches the strongest measured swell in this file, then recedes. Hear the withdrawal as part of the same phrase: the climax does not supply a lasting, full-orchestra conclusion.
cues.evidence: 11:10 is the loudest five-second window at −4.7 dB; by 11:30 the level is −22.5 dB, falling further towards 11:50. Relative levels compare passages within this recording only.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: A procession reduced to signals
cues.text: In the closing pages, the fanfare survives as fragments while the orchestral texture thins. The score eventually passes the call from trumpet to flute, leaving space around the remaining attacks.
cues.evidence: Peters pp. 45–47 show the diminishing texture, trumpet signals and final flute echo. The report’s 11:36 and 12:06 boundaries and low closing levels support a broad coda placement, not the exact transfer between instruments.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A plucked final punctuation
cues.text: At the end, listen for the distinction between fading resonance and the final plucked string punctuation. Mahler closes the march quietly rather than making the last return another orchestral climax.
cues.evidence: Peters p. 47 ends with a pizzicato string note after the trumpet/flute calls and bass-drum roll. The report is very quiet across 12:20–12:40; the final attack is not separately timed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The tread breaks into running motion
transitions.how: The funeral-march texture dwindles towards a quiet trumpet signal. Mahler interrupts that signal with a faster B♭-minor episode: the strings supply rapid running figures beneath a more extended trumpet line. The new pace and more continuous accompaniment break the procession’s tread, while dotted rhythms and rising leaps preserve links with the preceding music.
transitions.evidence: The 5:18 novelty maximum and 14 dB rise between the 5:15 and 5:20 windows locate the broad join. Peters p. 19 shows the fading march and signal; p. 25 shows the episode texture. Smoley’s guide identifies B♭ minor and the abrupt interruption.

transitions.title: The trumpet signal restores the procession
transitions.how: The faster episode’s crowded writing yields to the familiar trumpet rhythm. C♯ minor and the introductory fanfare recover their structural role before the march melody returns. Mahler does not simply repeat the episode more quietly: the running accompaniment gives way to the opening’s heavier, separated gestures, and the restored march is explicitly marked “Schwer”.
transitions.evidence: Boundaries at 6:52 and 6:58 follow the loud 6:35–6:45 crest; another swell at 7:15 precedes the quieter march region. The guide establishes the fanfare-to-march sequence; Peters p. 33 confirms Schwer. The marker locates the start of that broad return, not the Schwer bar.

transitions.title: The contrasting melody becomes a lament
transitions.how: The march subsides instead of being interrupted by a second identical outburst. Mahler reshapes the earlier episode’s melody into a slower, string-led lament in the A-minor region. Its rising leaps and falling seconds remain audible relatives of the earlier trumpet line, but the steadier pace brings the episode closer to the processional music.
transitions.evidence: The 9:50 trough and subsequent rise into 10:00–10:20 place the second episode approximately. The movement account identifies A minor; Smoley explains the transformation of the first trio’s trumpet theme. The harmony is not inferred from the report alone.

transitions.title: The climax leaves fragments of the call
transitions.how: The later climax falls away through sustained and descending lines. Fanfare rhythm reappears within the diminishing orchestral body, then breaks into separated calls. The closing pages reduce the sound further, from brass and strings to trumpet, flute and a distant bass-drum roll, before the final pizzicato punctuation. The join begins this withdrawal; it is not the moment of the flute’s last answer.
transitions.evidence: After the 11:10 maximum, levels fall through 11:30–11:50, with a boundary at 11:36. Peters pp. 45–47 establish the closing reduction and remaining instruments; the marker is a passage estimate.

source.title: Mahler, Symphony No. 5, I, Peters study score, plate 9015
source.locator: Printed pp. 3, 14, 25, 33, 45–47. Passage-level scoring snapshots, not continuous entry tracking; placements follow the report’s broad changes. The performance’s edition is unknown.

timeline.note: Opening score passage, p. 3: the first trumpet gives the call without accompaniment.
Opening-march passage, p. 14: woodwind and cello lines above march rhythm; approximate placement around the 4:02 change.
First-episode passage, p. 25: prominent trumpet above running violin figures; snapshot within the sustained 5:20–6:45 span.
Returning-march passage, p. 33: quiet woodwind melody and weighted brass punctuation; provisional placement after the 7:40 withdrawal.
Closing withdrawal, p. 45: trumpet figures persist among diminishing sustained parts; placed at the broad 11:36 change.
Final-page span, p. 47: trumpet and flute calls occur successively, with drum resonance and closing strings, not as a continuous tutti.

composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony anticipates Mahler’s so closely that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony. The cantata Das klagende Lied, written at eighteen and nineteen, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881, and Mahler turned to the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
